clinicalPearls: Syringomas are benign adnexal tumours of the eccrine sweat ducts presenting as multiple small, soft, skin-coloured to yellowish papules clustered on the lower eyelids and upper cheeks.
They are typically bilateral and symmetrical, appear around puberty or in early adulthood, and are commoner in women.
Individual papules are small and firm; they are usually asymptomatic and the concern is almost entirely cosmetic.
The periorbital region, especially the lower lids, is the classic site, and the clustered, symmetrical distribution is a helpful diagnostic clue.
There is a recognised association with Down syndrome, and an eruptive variant can appear on the trunk; diabetes has been linked to a clear-cell histological variant.
Diagnosis is usually clinical, but biopsy with histology confirms the characteristic ductal structures when there is doubt.

Treatment is for cosmesis only and is difficult, as lesions are dermal and multiple; options include ablative laser, electrocautery, excision and chemical peels, all with a tendency to recur and a risk of eyelid scarring.

Syringomas must be distinguished from xanthelasma, milia, sebaceous hyperplasia and, importantly, from the more aggressive microcystic adnexal carcinoma and morphoeic basal cell carcinoma when a lesion is solitary, indurated or growing.
reference.pathophysiology: Syringomas are benign proliferations (hamartomatous or adenomatous) of the intraepidermal eccrine sweat duct. Histology shows small ducts and solid epithelial cords embedded in a fibrous dermal stroma, with characteristic comma-shaped or tadpole-like ductal profiles lined by two layers of cuboidal cells. The proliferation is confined to the superficial to mid dermis without invasion, and hormonal influence is implicated by the tendency to appear or worsen around puberty and in women. Because the lesions are dermal and multifocal, they neither regress spontaneously nor respond to superficial treatment, and their depth explains the difficulty of complete cosmetic clearance.
additionalDifferentials: Trichoepithelioma and other benign adnexal tumours
Flat warts or lichen planus papules
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp and external examination of the periorbital distribution
Dermoscopy to assess surface and vascular pattern
Skin biopsy with histopathology when diagnosis is uncertain or a lesion is atypical
External photography to document distribution and monitor after treatment
Evaluation for associated conditions (e.g. Down syndrome) where clinically indicated
Deeper or excisional biopsy if microcystic adnexal carcinoma is suspected
redFlags: A solitary, indurated, enlarging or ill-defined lesion suggesting microcystic adnexal carcinoma or morphoeic basal cell carcinoma
Ulceration, bleeding or loss of eyelashes
Rapid change in a previously stable lesion
Deep infiltration or recurrence after excision suggesting a more aggressive adnexal tumour
reference.prognosis: Benign with an excellent prognosis and no threat to vision; lesions persist indefinitely. Cosmetic treatment is often only partially effective and recurrence is common, with a risk of scarring on the delicate eyelid skin.
pitfalls: Confusing syringomas with xanthelasma and thereby missing an opportunity to counsel on lipids, or vice versa
Mistaking an infiltrative microcystic adnexal carcinoma for benign syringomas and delaying appropriate excision
Aggressive ablative treatment of lower-lid lesions causing scarring, dyspigmentation or ectropion
Promising complete cosmetic clearance despite the high recurrence rate of dermal lesions
Failing to biopsy an atypical or solitary lesion before cosmetic destruction
